chapter_title: Register Renaming and the Register File
chapter_summary:
Register renaming is the technique that enables out-of-order execution to avoid WAR and WAW hazards. It is the key innovation that allows processors to execute instructions out of order while maintaining correct results.

**The problem:**

In a sequential processor, if two instructions write to the same architectural register, a WAW hazard occurs. If a later instruction writes to a register before an earlier instruction reads it, a WAR hazard occurs. These hazards force the processor to stall.

For example:
```
ADD R1, R2, R3     # I1: writes to R1
MUL R4, R1, R5     # I2: reads R1 (RAW hazard, handled by forwarding)
SUB R1, R6, R7     # I3: writes to R1 (WAW hazard with I1)
DIV R8, R1, R9     # I4: reads R1 (WAR hazard with I3, but I3 is later in program order)
```

Without renaming, I3 must wait until I1 writes to R1. I4 must wait until I3 writes to R1. This serializes execution.

**The solution:**

Register renaming maps architectural registers to a larger set of physical registers. Each write to an architectural register is assigned a new physical register. Reads use the most recent mapping.

**Register renaming mechanism:**

1. **Register Map Table (RAT):** Maps each architectural register to its current physical register. When an instruction is decoded, the RAT is read to find the physical registers for the source operands. The destination architectural register is mapped to a new physical register from the free list.

2. **Free List:** A list of physical registers that are not currently in use. When an instruction is decoded, a free physical register is allocated for its destination. When the instruction commits, the old physical register is returned to the free list.

3. **Physical Register File (PRF):** The actual register file that holds the values. It is much larger than the architectural register file (e.g., 256 physical registers for 32 architectural registers).

**Example:**
```
Initial: RAT[R1] = P1, RAT[R2] = P2, RAT[R3] = P3, ...

ADD R1, R2, R3     # Allocate P10 for R1. Read P2, P3. Write to P10.
                   # RAT[R1] = P10. Old mapping (P1) saved for recovery.

MUL R4, R1, R5     # Read RAT[R1] = P10, RAT[R5] = P5. Allocate P11 for R4.
                   # Write to P11. RAT[R4] = P11.

SUB R1, R6, R7     # Allocate P12 for R1. Read P6, P7. Write to P12.
                   # RAT[R1] = P12. Old mapping (P10) saved for recovery.

DIV R8, R1, R9     # Read RAT[R1] = P12, RAT[R9] = P9. Allocate P13 for R8.
                   # Write to P13. RAT[R8] = P13.
```

All four instructions can execute in parallel because they write to different physical registers (P10, P11, P12, P13). There are no WAW or WAR hazards.

**Area and power implications:**

The physical register file is large (e.g., 256 entries × 64 bits = 16,384 bits). It requires many read and write ports to support multiple instructions per cycle. For a 4-way superscalar processor, the PRF might need 8 read ports and 4 write ports. Multi-ported register files are expensive in area and power.

The RAT is smaller but must be accessed every cycle. The free list requires a hardware queue or bitmap.

Modern processors use several techniques to reduce PRF power:
- **Register file banking:** Dividing the PRF into banks to reduce the number of ports per bank.
- **Clock gating:** Disabling unused register file entries.
- **Hierarchical register file:** A small, fast register file for frequently accessed registers and a larger, slower file for the rest.

screens.title: Register Renaming and the Register File
screens.subtitle: How mapping architectural registers to physical lockers removes write hazards and enables out-of-order execution

narration.text: In this lesson we will make a concrete connection between two ideas: hazards that force sequential execution, and the technique that removes them, register renaming. Register renaming maps each architectural register name to a larger set of physical registers. That simple idea lets the processor give each write its own physical destination, so multiple writes no longer collide. You will see the core machinery: a Register Alias Table that tracks the current mapping, a free list of available physical registers, and a large physical register file that actually stores values. We will also examine costs: a wide, multi-ported physical register file needs many transistors and ports, so real designs use banking, clock gating, and hierarchical files to save area and power. Along the way you'll work through a six-instruction example and a branch misprediction recovery to see how saved old mappings restore state. By the end you should be able to explain why renaming eliminates WAR and WAW hazards, design a simple RAT and free list flow, and reason about area versus performance trade-offs for the PRF.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Mapping architectural registers to distinct physical registers prevents write-after-write and write-after-read hazards, unlocking parallel, out-of-order execution.

Map architectural names to many physical registers so writes do not collide.
In this lesson

Explore Key Topics

Physical Registers

Recovery

Metaphor

Renaming separates names from storage. That separation removes write collisions and enables safe out-of-order execution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives focus your learning and map directly to the chapter content. First, you will explain how register renaming eliminates write-after-read and write-after-write hazards. That means being able to describe a concrete instruction sequence where renaming lets instructions proceed in parallel rather than stalling. Second, you will design a simple renaming mechanism: a Register Alias Table and a free list that hands out physical registers at decode and reclaims them at commit. This objective requires you to trace mappings and saved old mappings for recovery. Third, you will distinguish architectural registers, which are programmer-visible names, from physical registers, the larger storage resources the hardware uses. Understanding that difference clarifies why we need more physical registers than architectural ones. Fourth, you will analyze the area and power implications of a large physical register file and name common mitigation strategies such as banking and clock gating. Each objective links to a concrete competency milestone so you can verify understanding by tracing a six-instruction example and restoring state after a branch misprediction.

screens.title: What are WAR and WAW hazards?
screens.subtitle: Why writes can serialize execution without renaming

narration.text: Start by defining the hazards that renaming solves. A write-after-write hazard, or WAW, happens when two instructions both write to the same architectural register in program order. If the later writer overwrites the earlier writer's destination before the earlier one completes its write, the processor may produce incorrect ordering unless it preserves the program order at commit. A write-after-read hazard, or WAR, occurs when an earlier instruction intends to read a register but a later instruction writes to that same architectural register before the read completes. Without renaming, these hazards force the processor to stall or to enforce strict ordering. Consider the short example from the chapter: ADD writes R1, then MUL reads R1, then SUB writes R1 again, then DIV reads R1. Without renaming, SUB must wait for the first write to complete to avoid WAW with ADD, and DIV must wait because SUB is later in program order but writes the register used by DIV, creating a potential WAR. The real problem is that the name R1 is reused, and the hardware cannot distinguish which write corresponds to which program value. The misconception to avoid is thinking forwarding alone solves these hazards; forwarding handles RAW dependencies where a later instruction reads a value produced earlier, but forwarding does not prevent two writes or a later write affecting an earlier read. A key takeaway: hazards arise from name reuse, not from value movement. How will you spot WAW and WAR in a small program trace?

keyIdea.title: Hazard definition
keyIdea.text: WAW and WAR hazards come from reusing the same architectural name for multiple writes and reads; renaming separates name from storage to avoid them.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Hazards
WAW and WAR hazards
When name reuse forces serialization.
Example instruction sequence
ADD R1, R2, R3     # I1: writes to R1
MUL R4, R1, R5     # I2: reads R1 (RAW handled by forwarding)
SUB R1, R6, R7     # I3: writes to R1 (WAW with I1)
DIV R8, R1, R9     # I4: reads R1 (WAR with I3)
Without renaming these writes and reads can force stalls and serialize execution.
Misconception
Forwarding fixes RAW hazards but does not solve WAW or WAR because those arise from name reuse, not the need to forward a produced value.
Check your understanding
Given three writes to the same register in flight, which hazards require renaming to avoid serialization?
Analogy: lockers and name tags
If two people wear the same name tag and put items into the same locker, collisions occur. Renaming gives each write a new locker so items do not conflict.
Key takeaway
Hazards are caused by name reuse. Removing name reuse removes the hazards.

screens.title: How register renaming works
screens.subtitle: RAT lookup, allocate from the free list, and update mappings

narration.text: Register renaming proceeds in a predictable sequence each time a writer is decoded. First, the Register Alias Table, or RAT, is consulted for source operands. The RAT gives the current physical registers that hold the logical register values the instruction will read. Second, for the instruction's destination, the rename stage allocates a fresh physical register from the free list. The instruction's destination architectural register is then mapped to that new physical register in the RAT, and the old mapping is saved for recovery. Third, the instruction executes using physical register identifiers and writes its result into the newly allocated physical register. Finally, when the instruction commits, the old physical register mapping can be returned to the free list. A concrete consequence is that multiple writes to the same architectural register receive distinct physical registers, so they no longer conflict. A common implementation detail is that the free list must be able to allocate multiple physical registers per cycle in wide pipelines; it can be a queue or a bitmap allocator. A misconception to avoid: the RAT is not the PRF — it is a small table mapping names to storage. The RAT is accessed every rename stage and must be fast. Now think about how this flow preserves precise state in the face of exceptions and mispredictions.

keyIdea.title: Rename flow
keyIdea.text: At decode: read RAT for sources, allocate new physical for destination, update RAT, save old mapping for recovery; free old physical at commit.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Rename Flow
Rename mechanism steps
A stable per-instruction sequence that preserves precise state.
1. Read RAT for sources
Use the RAT mappings to find physical source registers used during execution.
2. Allocate from free list
Pick a free physical register for the destination and mark it allocated for this instruction.
3. Update RAT and save old mapping
RAT[arch] = new physical. Save old physical so a misprediction can restore the previous state.
4. Execute and commit
Execution writes to the new physical register. At commit, free the saved old mapping back to the free list.
Concrete allocator choices
  • Queue-based free list: easy to implement, allocate in order.
  • Bitmap allocator: supports random access and multi-issue allocation but needs priority logic.
Remember: the free list must support the pipeline width and how many destinations are renamed per cycle.
Key Takeaway

Rename decouples names from storage using a quick RAT lookup and a free-list allocation; saved old mappings preserve recoverability.

screens.title: Register Alias Table (RAT) and saved mappings
screens.subtitle: How the RAT tracks current mappings and supports recovery

narration.text: The Register Alias Table is a small, fast table that maps every architectural register name to its current physical register number. The RAT is consulted at rename for each source operand so the processor knows which physical register to read. When a destination is renamed, the RAT entry for that architectural register is updated to the new physical register and the previous mapping is pushed to a recovery structure or saved in a checkpoint. That save is essential: if a branch is mispredicted or an exception occurs, the processor restores the RAT to the earlier mapping so subsequent instruction decoding sees the correct state. A common misconception is to think the RAT requires the same capacity as the physical file; it does not. The RAT holds one mapping per architectural register, so it is small (for example, 32 entries for a 32-register ISA), but it is read and updated every cycle. The saved old mappings are typically stored in the reorder buffer or in a dedicated checkpoint structure. Concretely, when instruction I allocates P10 for R1, RAT[R1] becomes P10 and the old P1 is recorded. If we mispredict after several renames, these saved mappings are used to rebuild RAT quickly. How would you implement the saved mapping store in your design?

keyIdea.title: RAT responsibilities
keyIdea.text: RAT maps names to physical registers and must save old mappings so the processor can restore state after misprediction or exception.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › RAT & Recovery
Register Alias Table and recovery
A compact map used on every rename operation.
Properties of the RAT
  • One entry per architectural register; small and fast.
  • Read at rename for sources; written at rename for destination mapping updates.
  • Old mapping must be saved to permit precise recovery after speculatively executing instructions.
Saved mapping example
If RAT[R1] = P1 and ADD allocates P10 for R1, update RAT[R1] = P10 and record P1 as the old mapping for recovery.
Checkpoint options
Reorder buffer stores old mappings per writer.
Checkpointed RAT copies allow fast restore for broader speculative windows.
Design trade-off: storing full RAT checkpoints is faster to restore but uses area; per-instruction saved mappings use less area but slower recovery logic.
Key Takeaway

Keep the RAT small and fast; save old mappings per rename so precise state can be restored after speculation is undone.

screens.title: Physical Register File (PRF)
screens.subtitle: What the PRF stores and why it is expensive

narration.text: The physical register file is the hardware storage array that actually holds values in the renamed system. Unlike the RAT, the PRF contains many entries—often an order of magnitude more than the architectural register count—so there are fresh physical registers available for many in-flight writes. For example, a design might have 256 physical registers for 32 architectural registers. The PRF must support multiple simultaneous reads and writes per cycle in a wide superscalar core; this requirement makes it expensive in both area and power. Multi-ported register files require additional read and write circuitry for each port, which increases transistor count and routing complexity. Designers mitigate these costs with register file banking, which splits the PRF into smaller banks each with fewer ports; clock gating, which disables parts of the file when inactive; and hierarchical register files, where a small fast file sits nearest the execution units and a larger slower file holds the rest. A common misconception is that more physical registers always improve performance. In reality, after a point, the area and power costs outweigh marginal speculative benefit. A good design balances enough physical registers to keep the pipeline fed while using banking and gating to manage cost. Consider how many read and write ports your PRF needs for a four-way issue core and how banking could reduce the per-bank port count.

keyIdea.title: PRF trade-offs
keyIdea.text: The PRF stores renamed values and demands many ports; banking, clock gating, and hierarchy reduce power and area at the cost of complexity and potential bank conflicts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Physical Register File
Physical Register File
Storage for all renamed values; multi-ported and costly.
Cost drivers
  • Number of entries (e.g., 256 entries × 64 bits). Larger files use more area.
  • Number of read/write ports. Each additional port adds complexity and power.
  • Access frequency. The PRF is read often and must be kept low-power.
Mitigation techniques
Register file banking, clock gating, and hierarchical files reduce per-access cost at the cost of complexity or conflicts.
Common trade-off
Banking reduces ports per bank but can introduce bank conflicts when multiple accesses hit the same bank in a cycle.
Design question
For a 4-way superscalar core you might need 8 read ports and 4 write ports. How would you bank a 256-entry PRF to reduce per-bank port count?
Example: split into 4 banks of 64 entries. Each bank needs fewer ports, but you must consider arbitration for bank conflicts.
Key Takeaway

The PRF is the main storage cost in renaming; its design balances ports, entries, power, and the risk of bank conflicts.

screens.title: Renaming example: P10, P11, P12, P13
screens.subtitle: Trace RAT updates and parallel execution in the example from the chapter

narration.text: Let's walk through the concrete example used in the chapter to make renaming tangible. Initially, architectural registers map to physical registers such as RAT[R1] = P1, RAT[R2] = P2, RAT[R3] = P3, and so on. When ADD R1, R2, R3 is renamed, the rename stage allocates P10 for the destination R1 and updates RAT[R1] = P10; it also records that the old mapping P1 is saved for recovery. Next, MUL R4, R1, R5 reads RAT[R1] = P10, so it will use the value that ADD writes to P10; it allocates P11 for R4. Then SUB R1, R6, R7 allocates P12 for R1 and writes its result there, updating RAT[R1] = P12 and saving P10 as the previous mapping to restore if needed. Finally DIV R8, R1, R9 reads RAT[R1] = P12 and allocates P13 for R8. The important consequence is that all four instructions can execute in parallel because they write to different physical registers P10, P11, P12, and P13. There is no WAW or WAR on the physical file. A typical misconception is believing values become immediately visible to older readers; instead, a reader uses the mapping that was current when it was renamed, which preserves correct data flow. Now examine the code panel to see the sequence and the mapping actions recorded for recovery.

keyIdea.title: Parallel writes
keyIdea.text: Distinct physical registers for each write allow the instructions to proceed in parallel without WAW or WAR hazards.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Worked Example
Example trace
Follow RAT updates and allocations.
Initial: RAT[R1]=P1, RAT[R2]=P2, RAT[R3]=P3, ...

ADD R1, R2, R3     # Allocate P10 for R1. Read P2, P3. Write to P10.
                  # RAT[R1] = P10. Old mapping (P1) saved for recovery.

MUL R4, R1, R5     # Read RAT[R1] = P10, RAT[R5] = P5. Allocate P11 for R4.
                  # Write to P11. RAT[R4] = P11.

SUB R1, R6, R7     # Allocate P12 for R1. Read P6, P7. Write to P12.
                  # RAT[R1] = P12. Old mapping (P10) saved for recovery.

DIV R8, R1, R9     # Read RAT[R1] = P12, RAT[R9] = P9. Allocate P13 for R8.
                  # Write to P13. RAT[R8] = P13.
Why this avoids hazards
  • Each destination gets a new physical register, so writes never target the same physical entry.
  • Readers use the mapping that existed when they were renamed, so they see the correct producer.
  • Saved old mappings allow restoration if later speculation is invalidated.
Key Takeaway

By allocating distinct physical registers per write, renaming removes WAW and WAR hazards and allows parallel execution.

screens.title: Six-instruction simulation (setup)
screens.subtitle: Assumptions and initial mapping for the hands-on exercise

narration.text: Before we simulate the six-instruction sequence, set clear initial conditions. We assume eight architectural registers R0 through R7 and sixteen physical registers P0 through P15. R0 is hardwired to P0 and serves as zero; initial RAT maps R1 through R7 to P1 through P7. The free list initially contains P8 through P15. The instruction stream we will trace is: ADD R1, R2, R3; MUL R4, R1, R5; SUB R1, R6, R7; AND R2, R1, R4; OR R3, R2, R1; ADD R5, R3, R4. For each instruction you will perform the rename steps: read RAT for sources, allocate a free physical register for the destination, update RAT, and save the old mapping so you can later restore it on misprediction. Track which physical registers are allocated and which are later freed at commit. I will walk through the first three instructions in the next screens and demonstrate how the RAT and free list evolve. Keep in mind the learning goal: show how renaming eliminates WAW and WAR and how saved old mappings allow recovery to a prior RAT state. Six-instruction simulation (setup) means 8 architectural regs (r0–r7), 16 physical regs (p0–p15), free list p8–p15, and a six-instruction stream to trace.. In practical terms, assumptions and initial mapping for the hands-on exercise. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Simulate instructions 1–3
screens.subtitle: Trace allocations and RAT updates for the first three instructions

narration.text: We now simulate the first three instructions and record RAT and free-list changes. Start state: RAT[R1]=P1, RAT[R2]=P2, RAT[R3]=P3, RAT[R4]=P4, RAT[R5]=P5, RAT[R6]=P6, RAT[R7]=P7; free list contains P8–P15. Instruction 1: ADD R1, R2, R3. Rename allocates P8 for R1 (first free), so RAT[R1] becomes P8 and P1 is saved as the old mapping. Sources read P2 and P3. Instruction 2: MUL R4, R1, R5. Rename reads RAT[R1]=P8 (so MUL will use the value ADD produces in P8), and allocates P9 for R4; RAT[R4]=P9 and old mapping P4 is saved. Instruction 3: SUB R1, R6, R7. Rename allocates P10 for R1, RAT[R1]=P10, and saves P8 as the old mapping. At this point the free list contains P11–P15. All three writes target different physical registers (P8, P9, P10), so they can execute in parallel without WAW or WAR hazards. A common student mistake is forgetting to save the old mapping; if you do not save P8 after SUB, you cannot restore RAT to the state before SUB on a misprediction. Next we will show a misprediction after the third instruction and how to restore RAT using saved mappings.

keyIdea.title: Trace update
keyIdea.text: After three instructions RAT[R1]=P10, RAT[R4]=P9; allocated P8, P9, P10; free list P11–P15; old mappings P1 and P8 saved.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Simulation 1–3
Instruction trace 1–3
Record RAT, allocations, and saved old mappings.
Step results
After ADD R1, R2, R3: Allocated P8 for R1. RAT[R1]=P8. Saved old mapping P1.
After MUL R4, R1, R5: Read RAT[R1]=P8. Allocated P9 for R4. RAT[R4]=P9. Saved old mapping P4.
After SUB R1, R6, R7: Allocated P10 for R1. RAT[R1]=P10. Saved old mapping P8.
State summary
Allocated physical registers: P8, P9, P10. Free list now: P11–P15. RAT reflects the latest mappings; old mappings stored for recovery.
If you forgot to save P8 when SUB renamed R1, you could not restore RAT to the state before SUB on a misprediction. Always save the previous mapping at rename.
Key Takeaway

Track allocations and saved old mappings precisely; those saved entries are the keys to correct recovery.

screens.title: Branch misprediction recovery
screens.subtitle: Restoring the RAT using saved old mappings

narration.text: A branch misprediction requires restoring the architectural state to the point before the mispredicted branch. In a renamed machine that means restoring the RAT so subsequent decode uses the original mappings. Using the hands-on trace, suppose the branch misprediction is detected after the third instruction (SUB) has been renamed. The processor looks up the saved old mappings pushed when instructions were renamed: SUB saved P8 as the old mapping for R1; ADD saved P1; MUL saved P4, and so on. To recover the RAT it walks the saved mappings in reverse program order and restores the RAT entries to their saved values. For example, restore RAT[R1] = P8 (undo SUB), then restore RAT[R4] = P4 (undo MUL), and finally RAT[R1] = P1 (undo ADD) if needed depending on the misprediction point. After restoring RAT, the free list must be reconstructed to reflect which physical registers are free. That reconstruction can be done by returning allocated registers for all squashed instructions or by using checkpointed free-list state. A common mistake is to forget to undo RAT updates in the correct reverse order; doing so can leave a newer mapping in place and corrupt subsequent renames. The closing question: how does the saved mapping order relate to commit order and why do we restore in reverse program order?

keyIdea.title: Recovery principle
keyIdea.text: Restore RAT entries using saved old mappings in reverse program order; reconstruct the free list accordingly to maintain precise state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Mispredict Recovery
Restoring state after misprediction
Use saved old mappings to rebuild the RAT and free list.
Restore steps
1. Walk saved mappings for squashed instructions in reverse program order.
2. For each saved mapping, write the old physical register back into the RAT entry.
3. Rebuild or restore the free list so freed physical registers become available again.
Why reverse order?
Restoring in reverse program order ensures that earlier saved mappings are not overwritten by later ones during the restore. It matches the natural undo sequence of speculative updates.
If saved mappings are stored in the reorder buffer, the RB's natural program order and squash logic make restoration straightforward.
Key Takeaway

Saved old mappings make correct recovery possible; restore RAT entries in reverse program order and repair the free list to resume decoding safely.

screens.title: Allocator designs and free-list implementations
screens.subtitle: Queue vs bitmap and multi-issue allocation trade-offs

narration.text: Allocating physical registers requires hardware that can hand out one or more free physical register identifiers per cycle. Two common choices are a queue-based free list and a bitmap allocator. A queue-based free list is simple: free registers are placed into a FIFO and popped when needed. It is straightforward to implement and to return registers at commit. However, supporting multiple allocations per cycle requires a wider queue interface. A bitmap allocator encodes free/allocated state in a vector and uses priority logic to choose free entries; it can support parallel allocation patterns but needs more complex combinational logic. The choice affects the pipeline's ability to rename several destinations in a single cycle and the latency and area of the allocator. Another trade-off is whether to checkpoint the free list or reconstruct it from the set of in-use physical registers at recovery. Checkpointing simplifies recovery but uses area; reconstruction is slower but area-efficient. A common misconception is that a bitmap always outperforms a queue; in practice, design constraints and how many simultaneous allocations are needed determine the best option. If your pipeline renames four destinations per cycle, examine how each allocator supports that width and how it reconvenes freed registers at commit.

keyIdea.title: Allocator trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Queues are simple but require wider interfaces for multi-issue; bitmaps support parallel allocation but cost combinational logic and area.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Free-list Design
Free-list allocator options
Queue and bitmap each have strengths and weaknesses.
Queue-based free list
Simple FIFO, easy to implement and to return registers at commit. Needs wider pop interface for multi-issue renames.
Bitmap allocator
Vector of free bits and priority logic to select multiple free entries. Supports parallel allocation but increases combinational area and power.
Checkpointing vs reconstruction
Checkpointing the free list enables fast recovery but consumes area. Reconstructing from in-use registers is slower but area-efficient.
Designers choose based on pipeline width, expected misprediction frequency, and area budget.
Key Takeaway

Choose allocators with your rename bandwidth and recovery latency in mind: queue simplicity vs bitmap parallelism.

screens.title: How many physical registers are needed?
screens.subtitle: Estimate minimum size and why designers often provision more

narration.text: Sizing the physical register file is an engineering decision guided by the number of architectural registers and the maximum number of in-flight writers that have not yet committed. The chapter gives a clear minimum formula: the minimum number of physical registers must be at least the number of architectural registers plus the number of in-flight instructions that will allocate new physical registers before commit. For example, with 32 architectural registers and a reorder buffer that can hold 128 in-flight writers, the minimum is 32 + 128 = 160 physical registers. Designers often provide more physical registers than this minimum to give the rename allocator headroom when multiple instructions write to many architectural registers, and to handle microarchitectural behaviors such as multi-precision or multi-write operations. However, increasing the PRF size and the number of ports increases area and power and may demand extra banking. A useful way to think about this trade-off is that extra physical registers reduce rename stalls from free-list exhaustion but increase cost. When evaluating a design, ask: how often does the free list run empty under realistic workloads, and what is the incremental performance gain versus the added area and power?

keyIdea.title: Sizing rule
keyIdea.text: Minimum physical registers = architectural registers + maximum in-flight writers before commit; designers typically add margin.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Sizing PRF
Estimating PRF size
A simple minimum formula gives a practical baseline.
Minimum example
With 32 architectural registers and a reorder buffer of 128 entries capable of holding writers, the minimum number of physical registers is 32 + 128 = 160.
Designers often provision more than the minimum to avoid free-list exhaustion during bursts of writer activity, at the cost of added area and power.
Practical trade-off
Extra physical registers reduce stalls but increase PRF complexity. Evaluate workload behavior to choose the best balance.
Ask yourself: does the expected working set of speculative writers justify extra registers, or is banking and architecture tuning a better investment?
Key Takeaway

Use the formula to set a minimum and then weigh performance gains against area and power costs when adding margin.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, register renaming eliminates WAR and WAW hazards by mapping each architectural write to a fresh physical register; this separation of name and storage is the foundation of safe out-of-order execution. Second, the Register Alias Table holds the current mapping from architectural names to physical registers and must save old mappings so the processor can restore state after misprediction or exception. Third, the free list is the allocator that hands out physical registers and must support the pipeline's rename width; its design—queue or bitmap—affects area and allocation latency. Fourth, the physical register file stores renamed values and often needs many read and write ports, making it expensive in area and power. Designers mitigate cost with register file banking, clock gating, and hierarchical register files, each with trade-offs. Keep these concepts linked: renaming removes hazards, but it shifts complexity into the RAT, allocator, and PRF design. A good mental model is name tags and lockers: names are tags, physical registers are lockers, RAT is the directory, and the free list is the pile of unused lockers.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Renaming separates names from storage; RAT, free list, and PRF implement it, and banking or gating reduce PRF cost.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Register renaming
Eliminates WAW and WAR by allocating fresh physical registers per write.
RAT vs PRF
RAT maps names to physical registers; PRF stores the values and needs many ports.
Free list & recovery
Free list allocates physical registers; old mappings must be saved to restore RAT on squash.
Summary takeaway
Renaming enables out-of-order execution by separating names from storage, but it shifts complexity to mapping, allocation, and the physical register file design—trade-offs designers must balance.

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for implementation and analysis

narration.text: Three compact reminders to use when designing or analyzing renaming hardware. First: always separate name and storage. That prevents WAW and WAR hazards because each write gets a fresh physical destination. Second: save old RAT entries at rename and restore them on misprediction; this is how the machine keeps precise state. Third: balance PRF size and port count against area and power—use banking and clock gating as necessary, but be mindful of bank conflicts and recovery complexity. Use these rules of thumb when you size the free list, choose an allocator, or evaluate the cost of extra ports. They will guide both correctness and efficient hardware design. Quick Reference means separate names from storage, save mappings for recovery, and balance prf size versus area/power using banking and gating.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for implementation and analysis. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Separate names from storage, save mappings for recovery, and balance PRF size versus area/power using banking and gating.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Quick Reference
Separate names & storage
Allocate a new physical register for each write so names do not collide.
Save old mappings
Use saved old RAT entries or checkpoints to restore precise state after squashes.
Balance PRF costs
Consider banking, clock gating, and hierarchy to trade area and power against latency and conflicts.
Final thought
Renaming is the enabler of out-of-order execution, but its hardware cost must be carefully managed with allocator and PRF design choices.
